source_tag: Composite — early-childhood scaffolding/frustration-tolerance guidance. Not a specific cited study.

source_tag: Composite — early-childhood frustration/task-persistence coaching guidance. Not a specific cited study.

options.rationale: Responds to the louder cue rather than the higher-risk one.

options.rationale: Fails to act on a visible physical safety risk.

options.label: D

source_tag: Composite — equity guidance against grading decisions influenced by anticipated student pushback. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student, frustrated after a disappointing mock-test result, snaps angrily at a classmate who tried to offer sympathy, causing visible hurt.

options.text: Steps in calmly, gives the frustrated student a moment to cool down privately, and separately checks on the hurt classmate afterward

options.label: B
options.text: Publicly tells the frustrated student to 'control themselves' in front of the class

options.label: C

source_tag: Composite — exam-stress-driven interpersonal de-escalation guidance for Class 12 students. Not a specific cited study.

options.label: B

options.rationale: Escalates rather than de-escalates a heated but private moment.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Jumps to a formal consequence without attempting the lower-cost de-escalation options first.

source_tag: Composite — private-confrontation de-escalation guidance for higher-secondary grade disputes. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: During a stressful revision period, two Class 12 students in the same friend group have a falling-out that spills into visible tension during a group study session the teacher is supervising.

options.label: A
options.text: Calmly acknowledges the tension without forcing reconciliation, and gives both space to work separately if needed for that session
options.rationale: De-escalates by not forcing an unready resolution while still accommodating both students' needs.

options.label: B

options.label: D

source_tag: Composite — peer-conflict accommodation guidance for stressed higher-secondary group study settings. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student asks a highly specific, advanced question that goes beyond the syllabus, revealing genuine intellectual curiosity rather than exam anxiety.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.rationale: Shuts down curiosity by citing syllabus scope alone.

options.rationale: Risks spreading misinformation rather than admitting a knowledge limit.

options.label: D
options.text: Discourages the question, saying it will 'waste time' better spent on exam prep
options.rationale: Discourages genuine intellectual engagement in favor of narrow exam focus.

source_tag: Composite — beyond-syllabus curiosity engagement guidance for higher-secondary science/humanities classrooms. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 11 student repeatedly asks doubts framed around 'what will actually be asked in the exam' rather than understanding the concept, suggesting a purely score-driven mindset.

options.label: A
options.text: Answers the exam-relevance question honestly, but also gently connects it to genuine understanding, without shaming the score-focused framing
options.rationale: Meets the student where they are while still nudging toward deeper understanding, without judgment.

options.label: B
options.text: Answers only the exam-relevance part every time, reinforcing a purely transactional relationship with the material
options.rationale: Resolves the doubt but doesn't attempt to build any deeper engagement.

options.label: C
options.text: Refuses to answer 'exam-only' framed questions, insisting the student ask about understanding instead
options.rationale: Withholds a legitimate answer over a framing preference.

options.label: D
options.text: Criticizes the student for 'only caring about marks' instead of answering the actual doubt
options.rationale: Criticizes the student's motivation rather than resolving their doubt.

source_tag: Composite — score-oriented-question engagement guidance for higher-secondary exam-pressure classrooms. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student asks a doubt about a topic just days before the board exam that reveals a significant, previously undiscovered gap in a core area.

options.rationale: Accurately assesses the difficulty but offers nothing actionable.

options.text: Downplays the gap's significance just to avoid alarming the student, without actually addressing it
options.rationale: Prioritizes the student's emotional comfort over giving them what could still help.

options.label: D
options.text: Reacts with visible alarm, which increases the student's panic without adding any useful help
options.rationale: Reacts in a way that increases distress without providing any actual assistance.

source_tag: Composite — last-minute-gap-discovery response guidance for board-exam-proximate doubts. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student's chosen career path requires a niche skill the standard curriculum doesn't cover, and they ask for guidance the syllabus wasn't designed to give.

options.label: A

options.rationale: Adapts her role usefully within honest limits, connecting the student to better-suited resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Tells the student this isn't part of her job and declines to help at all
options.rationale: Declines to engage at all with a legitimate student need.

options.rationale: Risks giving poor guidance in an area outside her actual expertise.

options.label: D
options.text: Redirects the student to focus only on syllabus-relevant goals, dismissing the niche interest
options.rationale: Dismisses a genuine interest rather than adapting to support it appropriately.

source_tag: Composite — beyond-curriculum career-guidance adaptation guidance for higher-secondary students with niche goals. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 11 lab session designed for pairs doesn't work well because of an odd number of students that day, and the plan doesn't account for it.

options.label: A

options.rationale: Adapts the grouping and task on the spot so everyone can meaningfully participate.

options.label: B

options.rationale: Leaves one student to attempt a paired task alone without adjustment.

options.rationale: Cancels a whole session over a solvable logistical mismatch.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Excludes a student entirely rather than finding a workable adaptation.

source_tag: Composite — group-size-mismatch adaptation guidance for higher-secondary lab sessions. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 revision plan was designed assuming five remaining weeks before boards, but a sudden school closure removes a full week from the schedule.

options.label: A
options.text: Re-prioritizes the revision plan for the highest-yield topics given the reduced time, communicating the adjusted plan clearly to students
options.rationale: Adapts the plan intelligently to the real time constraint, prioritizing what matters most.

options.rationale: Tries to preserve everything at the cost of depth and retention.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Abandons the planning responsibility entirely under pressure.

source_tag: Composite — time-constraint revision-plan re-prioritization guidance for board-exam preparation. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 11 student discloses they're considering dropping out of the stream entirely mid-year, a decision with major consequences, and asks the teacher for advice on the spot.

options.rationale: Handles a high-stakes, ambiguous request for advice by supporting reasoning rather than dictating an answer, with appropriate escalation.

options.label: B
options.text: Tells the student definitively what to do based on her own opinion, without exploring the student's own reasoning first
options.rationale: Imposes her own view on a major life decision without exploring the student's actual reasoning.

options.label: C
options.text: Says 'that's a big decision, think about it yourself' without engaging further
options.rationale: Disengages from a request for real guidance on something significant.

options.label: D
options.text: Discourages the idea immediately without hearing the student's reasoning
options.rationale: Shuts down the idea without understanding it first.

source_tag: Composite — high-stakes-decision support guidance for stream-change requests in higher-secondary settings. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student asks to be excused from a mandatory internal assessment for an unspecified 'personal reason' close to the exam, without further detail, and the policy requires a documented reason.

options.label: A
options.text: Respects their privacy while explaining the documentation requirement, and offers a private, low-pressure way to share only what's needed to process the request
options.rationale: Balances institutional requirements with respect for privacy on a sensitive matter.

options.label: B
options.text: Demands the full personal reason before considering the request at all
options.rationale: Demands full disclosure of what may be a legitimately private matter.

options.label: C
options.text: Waives the requirement entirely without any documentation, setting an inconsistent precedent
options.rationale: Skips policy entirely, which risks inconsistency for future similar requests.

options.label: D
options.text: Denies the request outright since no reason was given
options.rationale: Rejects a potentially legitimate request without exploring a way to meet both needs.

source_tag: Composite — privacy-respecting policy-compliance guidance for sensitive personal-reason requests in higher-secondary settings. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: Two Class 11 students in the same friend group both want to be nominated for a single limited leadership opportunity, and both have comparable, strong qualifications.

options.label: A
options.text: Uses a clear, pre-defined, transparent criterion (structured interview or brief proposal) to decide, explained to both beforehand
options.rationale: Makes a transparent, criteria-based decision when two strong candidates compete for one spot.

options.label: B
options.text: Picks based on personal rapport with one student, without a stated process
options.rationale: Decides based on unstated personal preference rather than a fair process.

options.label: C
options.text: Avoids deciding at all by not nominating either student
options.rationale: Avoids a real decision responsibility, potentially disadvantaging both students.

options.label: D
options.text: Lets the two students 'sort it out between themselves' for a decision that's actually the teacher's to make
options.rationale: Offloads a decision that should be made using clear criteria onto the students' peer dynamic.

source_tag: Composite — transparent-selection-criteria guidance for competitive, comparably-qualified leadership nominations. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student known for careful, thorough work has started submitting assignments with careless errors uncharacteristic of their usual standard, right during peak exam-preparation season.

options.label: A
options.text: Considers burnout, sleep, and overload as likely explanations given the timing, and checks in privately before assuming reduced effort
options.rationale: Connects the timing (peak exam season) to a likely cause (burnout/overload) before assuming a motivational explanation.

options.label: B
options.text: Marks the errors down at face value without considering the seasonal timing as a possible factor
options.rationale: Grades the output without considering an obvious contextual factor.

options.label: C
options.text: Assumes the student has 'gotten complacent' and comments on it without further inquiry
options.rationale: Assigns a character explanation without checking a very plausible seasonal cause.

options.label: D
options.text: Publicly contrasts their current work with earlier, better work as a 'wake-up call'
options.rationale: Public comparison during a likely burnout period risks worsening the situation.

source_tag: Composite — seasonal-burnout root-cause diagnosis guidance for higher-secondary students in exam season. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 11 student who was enthusiastic about a specific elective has, over a month, started skipping just that one subject's optional sessions while attending everything else normally.

options.label: A
options.text: Investigates what's specific to that subject (a teacher conflict, a topic difficulty, a peer issue) rather than assuming general disengagement
options.rationale: Notices the subject-specific nature of the pattern, which points to a more targeted cause than general disengagement.

options.label: B
options.text: Assumes the student has generally become less motivated this term, without noting the subject-specific pattern
options.rationale: Misses the specificity of the pattern, defaulting to a broader, less accurate explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: Marks the absences without any inquiry into the subject-specific pattern
options.rationale: Records the outcome without investigating the specific, unusual pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Publicly asks the student in front of peers why they've stopped attending that specific elective
options.rationale: Puts the student on the spot publicly for what could be a sensitive, specific issue.

source_tag: Composite — subject-specific-disengagement root-cause diagnosis guidance for higher-secondary elective attendance. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A Class 12 student's parents report at a meeting that their child seems 'fine' at home, but the teacher has observed a clear, sustained decline in classroom engagement and mood over several weeks.

options.label: A
options.text: Shares the specific classroom observations factually with the parents, treating the discrepancy as worth understanding together rather than dismissing either view
options.rationale: Treats a genuine discrepancy between settings as informative rather than dismissing either data point.

options.label: B
options.text: Defers entirely to the parents' assessment since they know the child better, and stops monitoring the classroom pattern
options.rationale: Discounts her own direct, sustained observation in favor of a different-context report.

options.label: C
options.text: Insists her own observation is correct and the parents 'just aren't seeing it,' without further collaborative discussion
options.rationale: Dismisses the parents' perspective rather than exploring the discrepancy together.

options.label: D
options.text: Doesn't mention her observations at all, avoiding the discrepancy entirely
options.rationale: Withholds a real, relevant observation from the people best placed to help.

source_tag: Composite — cross-context-discrepancy root-cause diagnosis guidance (school vs. home observation) for higher-secondary students. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A junior teacher's approach to handling a student's exam-stress breakdown was well-intentioned but not fully effective, and they ask the senior teacher for feedback afterward.

options.rationale: Provides genuinely useful, specific, growth-oriented feedback that builds real capability.

options.label: B
options.text: Gives only vague praise without any specific, actionable feedback
options.rationale: Avoids the substantive feedback the junior teacher actually needs to improve.

options.label: C
options.text: Criticizes the handling harshly without acknowledging what was done well
options.rationale: Demoralizes without balancing the critique with what was done well.

options.label: D
options.text: Avoids giving any real feedback to prevent discomfort
options.rationale: Withholds feedback the junior teacher explicitly asked for.

source_tag: Composite — constructive-feedback mentorship guidance for junior-teacher crisis-response coaching. Not a specific cited study.

options.text: Facilitates a discussion that surfaces everyone's concerns, and helps the group converge on one clear, consistently applied standard
options.rationale: Builds genuine consensus and consistency through facilitation rather than imposition.

options.label: B
options.text: Imposes her own preferred approach on the department without hearing the other views
options.rationale: Resolves the inconsistency but at the cost of colleague buy-in and input.

options.rationale: Leaves a known inconsistency in place, which will confuse students and undermine the policy.

source_tag: Composite — departmental-consistency facilitation guidance for policy-enforcement disagreements among senior-secondary staff. Not a specific cited study.

options.rationale: Manages the parent relationship while preserving and building the junior teacher's standing and involvement.

options.rationale: Solves the immediate issue but erodes the junior teacher's authority and ownership.

options.label: C

options.rationale: Fails to address a legitimate parent concern at all.

options.text: Sides with the parent's framing immediately and criticizes the junior teacher without first hearing their side
options.rationale: Undermines a colleague's credibility without hearing their perspective first.

source_tag: Composite — bypass-escalation management guidance protecting junior-teacher authority in parent disputes. Not a specific cited study.

options.rationale: Allows an actual bias to affect the grade.

source_tag: Composite — conflict-of-interest management guidance for TA/instructor grading relationships in undergraduate settings. Not a specific cited study.

source_tag: Composite — equity guidance against communication-visibility bias in undergraduate grading and feedback. Not a specific cited study.

options.text: Notices the pattern but doesn't change anything, assuming it reflects genuine differences in preparation
options.rationale: Notices a real pattern but rationalizes it away rather than addressing it.

options.rationale: Overcorrects into an equally unbalanced treatment of specific students.

source_tag: Composite — seminar-discussion de-escalation guidance for personal academic disagreements among adult students. Not a specific cited study.

options.rationale: Escalates rather than de-escalates a heated but substantively valid complaint.

source_tag: Composite — public-group-conflict de-escalation guidance for undergraduate presentation settings. Not a specific cited study.

options.rationale: Under-resolves a legitimate doubt due to an unrelated time-management concern.

options.rationale: Fails to resolve a student's actual question, even if avoidable.

scenario: A course originally designed for in-person delivery has to shift to an online format mid-semester due to unforeseen circumstances, and the existing materials don't translate directly.

options.label: A
options.text: Redesigns the key interactive elements for the online format, preserving the core learning goals rather than just uploading the same slides
options.rationale: Genuinely redesigns for the new medium while preserving the actual learning goals.

options.label: B
options.text: Delivers the same slides in a video call format without adapting for the different medium
options.rationale: Changes the delivery channel without adapting the pedagogy to it.

options.label: C
options.text: Cancels interactive components entirely, reverting to pure lecture for the rest of the term
options.rationale: Drops valuable instructional elements rather than adapting them.

options.label: D
options.text: Makes no changes and expects students to adapt to a format the course wasn't designed for
options.rationale: No adaptation despite a real, significant format change.

source_tag: Composite — mid-semester delivery-format adaptation guidance for undergraduate courses. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A course includes both students fluent in the language of instruction and international/exchange students who are still building fluency, and a fast-paced discussion format is leaving some clearly behind.

options.label: A
options.text: Adds structured supports (written prompts in advance, slightly more processing time) that help all students without slowing down the discussion for fluent speakers
options.rationale: Adapts supports that genuinely help without penalizing either group.

options.label: B
options.text: Continues the same fast-paced format for everyone, assuming students should adapt to the language level of the course
options.rationale: Ignores a real access gap tied to language proficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: Slows the discussion dramatically for the whole class, frustrating fluent speakers
options.rationale: Solves one group's access at a real cost to the other's engagement.

options.label: D
options.text: Doesn't address the gap since language proficiency is 'not the instructor's responsibility'
options.rationale: Disclaims responsibility for a real, addressable access barrier.

source_tag: Composite — language-proficiency inclusive-adaptation guidance for undergraduate discussion-based courses. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A required software tool for a lab course turns out to be inaccessible to some students due to hardware/OS limitations, discovered a week into the course.

options.label: A
options.text: Finds and provides an equivalent alternative tool or access method (lab computer time, cloud-based option) so no student is excluded from the coursework
options.rationale: Actively solves the access barrier so all students can complete the actual coursework.

options.label: B
options.text: Tells the affected students to 'find a workaround' on their own
options.rationale: Places the burden of solving an institutional/course-design problem on the affected students.

options.label: C
options.text: Continues the course assuming everyone will eventually get access somehow
options.rationale: Ignores an active, confirmed access barrier.

options.label: D
options.text: Removes the tool-based component from the course entirely for everyone rather than solving the access issue
options.rationale: Removes a valuable learning component for everyone rather than solving a fixable access issue.

source_tag: Composite — technology-access-barrier resolution guidance for undergraduate lab courses. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A student requests an extension on a paper citing a mental-health-related struggle, without a formal medical note, close to the deadline.

options.label: A
options.text: Grants a reasonable, short extension in good faith consistent with how similar informal requests are handled, and points to formal support resources without demanding proof
options.rationale: Extends reasonable good faith consistent with policy while still connecting the student to appropriate support.

options.label: B
options.text: Demands a formal medical certificate before considering any extension
options.rationale: Demands documentation that may not be readily available for a sensitive, time-sensitive request.

options.label: C
options.text: Denies the request outright, assuming it's likely an excuse
options.rationale: Assumes bad faith on a sensitive disclosure without basis.

options.label: D
options.text: Grants an open-ended, unlimited extension without any defined boundary or follow-up
options.rationale: Fails to set any boundary, which can be unfair to other students and unhelpful to the requesting student's own planning.

source_tag: Composite — good-faith accommodation guidance for informally-disclosed mental-health-related extension requests in higher education. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A grading dispute arises where the instructor's own rubric is genuinely ambiguous on a specific point, and a student's answer could reasonably be scored either way.

options.label: A
options.text: Acknowledges the rubric's ambiguity honestly, applies a reasonable and consistent resolution, and notes the ambiguity for future rubric revisions
options.rationale: Handles genuine ambiguity honestly and improves the process for the future.

options.label: B
options.text: Insists the original score is correct without acknowledging the rubric's actual ambiguity
options.rationale: Defends a position without acknowledging a real flaw in the underlying rubric.

options.label: C
options.text: Changes the score just to end the dispute, without a principled basis for the new score either
options.rationale: Resolves the immediate conflict without any principled standard, risking future inconsistency.

options.label: D
options.text: Refuses to discuss the rubric at all, citing 'grading is final'
options.rationale: Refuses to engage with a legitimate question about the assessment's own clarity.

source_tag: Composite — rubric-ambiguity resolution guidance for undergraduate grading disputes. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A student in a group project reports that another group member hasn't contributed at all, but the non-contributing member says they were 'given nothing to do' by the rest of the group.

options.label: A
options.text: Talks to the whole group together to understand the actual dynamic before assigning any grade differentiation, rather than accepting either side's account alone
options.rationale: Investigates a genuinely two-sided, ambiguous claim before making a grading decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Accepts the complaining students' account fully and grades the accused member down without hearing their side
options.rationale: Acts on one account without hearing the other side of a disputed claim.

options.label: C
options.text: Splits the difference evenly without investigating either account
options.rationale: Avoids the actual investigation needed to make a fair, differentiated call.

options.label: D
options.text: Refuses to get involved in 'group dynamics,' grading everyone the same regardless of actual contribution
options.rationale: Ignores a real fairness concern about unequal contribution.

source_tag: Composite — disputed-group-contribution investigation guidance for undergraduate group projects. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A student's exam performance has been sharply inconsistent — excellent on some assessments, very poor on others — with no obvious pattern by topic difficulty.

options.label: A
options.text: Looks for patterns beyond topic difficulty (exam format, time of day, test anxiety, external circumstances) before concluding it's inconsistent effort
options.rationale: Investigates a genuinely puzzling pattern across multiple possible causes rather than assuming one.

options.label: B
options.text: Averages the scores and treats the student as 'middling' without investigating the inconsistency itself
options.rationale: Treats a meaningful pattern as noise by averaging it away.

options.label: C
options.text: Assumes the student is 'unreliable' and doesn't investigate further
options.rationale: Assigns a character judgment without investigating the actual variability.

options.label: D
options.text: Ignores the pattern since the overall grade still meets a passing threshold
options.rationale: Dismisses a genuinely interesting and possibly actionable pattern because the aggregate outcome looks fine.

source_tag: Composite — inconsistent-performance-pattern root-cause diagnosis guidance for undergraduate assessment analysis. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A significant portion of the class does poorly on the same exam question, despite the topic being covered clearly according to the instructor's own notes and recordings.

options.label: A
options.text: Reviews the actual delivered content and the question wording itself for a possible mismatch, before assuming a class-wide effort or ability problem
options.rationale: Investigates both the content delivery and the assessment design as possible sources of a systemic gap.

options.label: B
options.text: Assumes the class collectively didn't study that section and moves on without further review
options.rationale: Assumes a student-side cause without checking the instructional side.

options.label: C
options.text: Assumes the question was simply 'too hard' without checking whether it matched what was actually taught
options.rationale: Assumes question difficulty without verifying alignment to what was actually taught.

options.label: D
options.text: Curves the grades without investigating whether the underlying issue was in the teaching or the question design
options.rationale: Fixes the symptom (score distribution) without understanding or addressing the actual cause.

source_tag: Composite — instructor-side root-cause investigation guidance for systemic exam-question underperformance in higher education. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A previously punctual and well-prepared student has been arriving with incomplete readings for the past three sessions in a row, with no explanation given.

options.label: A
options.text: Reaches out respectfully, treating the student as an adult managing possibly competing demands, and asks open-endedly what's changed before assuming disengagement
options.rationale: Investigates a real, sustained pattern respectfully and without presuming a cause.

options.label: B
options.text: Notes the pattern in participation grades without any direct outreach to understand it
options.rationale: Records the outcome without any inquiry into a real change in a previously reliable student.

options.label: C
options.text: Assumes the student has 'lost interest' in the course and doesn't investigate further
options.rationale: Assumes disengagement without checking for other explanations (workload, personal circumstances).

options.label: D
options.text: Publicly comments in class on the pattern of incomplete readings without addressing it with the individual privately
options.rationale: Publicly comments on an individual pattern rather than addressing it privately, inappropriate for adult students.

source_tag: Composite — sustained-preparation-drop root-cause outreach guidance for undergraduate students. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: Multiple TAs grading the same assignment across sections are producing noticeably inconsistent scores for comparable work, and students have started comparing notes and complaining.

options.label: A
options.text: Runs a brief calibration session with all TAs using sample papers to align standards before further grading continues
options.rationale: Addresses a real fairness issue by building genuine shared standards among the grading team.

options.label: B
options.text: Tells TAs individually to 'be more consistent' without any structured calibration process
options.rationale: Names the problem without providing the structured process needed to actually fix it.

options.label: C
options.text: Re-grades everything herself without involving or developing the TAs' judgment
options.rationale: Solves the immediate fairness issue but removes the TAs' opportunity to develop consistent judgment.

options.label: D
options.text: Ignores the complaints since 'some variation is normal'
options.rationale: Dismisses a real equity issue affecting multiple students.

source_tag: Composite — grading-calibration leadership guidance for multi-TA course sections. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A junior faculty member wants to try an unconventional teaching method that carries some risk of not working well, and comes to a senior colleague for a green light.

options.label: A
options.text: Discusses the idea's merits and risks honestly, offers to help mitigate the biggest risks, and supports them trying it with a plan to evaluate afterward
options.rationale: Genuinely engages with the idea, helps manage risk, and supports thoughtful innovation.

options.label: B
options.text: Discourages any deviation from conventional methods, regardless of the idea's merit
options.rationale: Discourages innovation reflexively rather than evaluating the actual idea.

options.label: C
options.text: Approves it without any discussion of risks or how to evaluate whether it worked
options.rationale: Approves without adding any value through discussion or evaluation planning.

options.label: D
options.text: Tells them to 'just try it and see,' offering no substantive input either way
options.rationale: Offers no real mentorship input despite being asked for guidance.

source_tag: Composite — innovation-support mentorship guidance for junior faculty pedagogical experimentation. Not a specific cited study.

scenario: A TA reports feeling unsure how to handle a student who repeatedly challenges their authority in section, given the TA's relatively junior status compared to the students' expectations of a 'real professor.'

options.label: A
options.text: Coaches the TA on specific, practical strategies for asserting appropriate authority respectfully, and offers to be a visible resource if needed
options.rationale: Provides genuine, practical coaching that builds the TA's actual capability and confidence.

options.label: B
options.text: Tells the TA to 'just be more confident' without concrete, actionable guidance
options.rationale: Offers a platitude rather than concrete, usable strategies.

options.label: C
options.text: Takes over the TA's section personally to avoid the problem, without building the TA's capability
options.rationale: Solves the problem by removing the TA's role rather than developing them.

options.label: D
options.text: Dismisses the concern as something the TA should 'just handle,' without any support
options.rationale: Withholds support from someone who explicitly asked for help with a real challenge.

source_tag: Composite — authority-assertion coaching guidance for junior TAs facing student pushback. Not a specific cited study.
